title: Phishing Simulation
summary: A phishing simulation is an authorised exercise in which an organisation sends realistic but harmless lure messages to its own staff in order to measure and improve behaviour. The simulation platform records who opened, clicked, entered data on a teaching page, or reported the message through the report button, and never captures real credentials. The point is not the click rate on its own. Mature programmes track the reporting rate and the time to first report, because employee reporting is what turns a phishing message into a detection event for the security team. Simulations are only sound when they are paired with short training, a clear and blame free reporting policy, and a schedule that avoids live incidents and sensitive periods. Frequent uncontrolled simulations also create real operational cost: helpdesk volume rises, and a workforce that assumes every odd email is fake may ignore a genuine compromise. The most damaging mistake is naming and shaming the people who click, which suppresses reporting and destroys the very signal the programme exists to collect.

exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

beginner.definition: A phishing simulation is a practice fake email sent by your own company. It looks like a real scam message, but it is safe and it is tracked. The aim is to see how people react and to help them improve. No real password is ever collected.
beginner.whyItMatters: Fake messages are one of the most common ways attackers get in. People cannot be perfect, so the goal is to make reporting quick and easy. Practice helps staff spot common tricks before a real message arrives. It also tells the security team how many reports they should expect in a real event.
howItWorks: The security team picks a story that fits the company, such as a delivery or payroll notice.
They agree the rules first, such as who is included and when the messages may be sent.
The safe message is sent, and the system records who opened it and who clicked.
Anyone who clicks lands on a teaching page that explains the warning signs.
Staff are encouraged to report the message, and reports are counted as a good result.
The team reviews the numbers, adjusts the training, and plans the next round.
beginner.example: Imagine a lifeboat drill on a ship. Nobody is in danger and nobody is blamed for a slow start. The crew practises the steps so that a real alarm is not a surprise. Afterwards the captain checks how quickly the alarm was raised, not only how many people reached the deck. The drill is repeated, and the notes from each drill shape the next one.
takeaways: Report rate matters more than click rate alone.
Never punish people who click, because that stops all reporting.
Always agree the timing and rules before you send anything.

objectives: Explain what a phishing simulation is and why it must be authorised and harmless.
Identify the metrics a simulation programme should track beyond the click rate.
Describe how simulation results are linked to short training and to the report button.
Explain why blame and punishment undermine a simulation programme.
Describe the operational risks of running simulations badly, such as helpdesk overload.
Explain how a high reporting rate helps a security team respond to real campaigns.
